Designing reaction-cross-diffusion systems with Turing and wave instabilities

Edgardo Villar-Sepúlveda Email: edgardo.villar-sepulveda@bristol.ac.uk Affiliation: Engineering Mathematics, University of Bristol, Ada Lovelace Building, Tankard’s Cl, University Walk, Bristol, BS8 1TW, United Kingdom    Alan R. Champneys Email: a.r.champneys@bristol.ac.uk Affiliation: Engineering Mathematics, University of Bristol, Ada Lovelace Building, Tankard’s Cl, University Walk, Bristol, BS8 1TW, United Kingdom    Andrew L. Krause Email: andrew.krause@durham.ac.uk Affiliation: Mathematical Sciences Department, Durham University, Upper Mountjoy Campus, Stockton Rd, Durham DH1 3LE, United Kingdom
Abstract

General conditions are established under which reaction-cross-diffusion systems can undergo spatiotemporal pattern-forming instabilities. Recent work has focused on designing systems theoretically and experimentally to exhibit patterns with specific features, but the case of non-diagonal diffusion matrices has yet to be analysed. Here, a framework is presented for the design of general nn-component reaction-cross-diffusion systems that exhibit Turing and wave instabilities of a given wavelength. For a fixed set of reaction kinetics, it is shown how to choose diffusion matrices that produce each instability; conversely, for a given diffusion tensor, how to choose linearised kinetics. The theory is applied to several examples including a hyperbolic reaction-diffusion system, two different 3-component models, and a spatio-temporal version of the Ross-Macdonald model for the spread of malaria.

keywords
Reaction-diffusion; Diffusion-driven instability; Spatiotemporal oscillations; Turing instability; wave instability

1 Introduction

Spontaneous pattern formation in spatially extended systems has been widely studied following Turing’s 1952 paper [1] and remains an area of substantial current work both theoretically [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9], and in a variety of applied contexts [10, 11, 12, 13]. Substantial emphasis has been placed on 2-component reaction-diffusion equations, as these are the first and one of the simplest models of pattern formation [14]. Extensions to three and more component systems have also been carried out, largely using linear stability theory and direct numerical simulations [15, 16, 17, 18, 19]. Importantly, there has been substantially less work on systems with more than three species despite their ubiquity in many areas of application (e.g. gene regulatory networks responsible for key aspects of embryological development can include thousands of genes [20]); see [21, 22, 23] for examples of theoretical studies of nn-component reaction-diffusion systems.

In recent work, the first two authors developed general conditions under which an nn-component reaction-diffusion system can undergo Turing or wave instabilities [5], generalizing ideas from the 3-component case [17]. Given the linearized reaction kinetics of the system, the authors determined if there exists a diffusion tensor such that the system can admit Turing or wave instabilities, and if so provided a procedure for constructing a diagonal diffusion tensor for which these instabilities of specified wavelengths would emerge. These ideas are, in a sense, a generalization of the large-domain approximation used in the two-component case to determine ‘Turing conditions’ on pattern formation which are a function only of kinetic parameters and diffusion rates (see e.g. (14, Chapter 2)).

However, studying the stability of more general reaction-transport systems will not necessarily lead to diagonal diffusion tensors after linearization. Instead, it may give rise to a range of more complex linear operators. One well-studied class of such systems comprises reaction-cross-diffusion systems involving fluxes of some components influencing the growth rates of others. Such systems are becoming increasingly well-studied, particularly since the pioneering work of Keller and Segel [24] as well as Shigesada, Kawasaki, and Teramoto [25]; see [26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32] for some recent examples of reaction-cross-diffusion systems. Most of this work focuses again on the two or three-component cases, but there are no general results, to our knowledge, on linear instabilities for nn-component systems (along the same lines as [5, 21] for reaction-diffusion equations).

Part of the reason for this is that reaction-cross-diffusion systems are not as restrictive as classical reaction-diffusion systems in terms of conditions for pattern formation; for example, cross-diffusion terms can induce Turing instabilities in systems with two self-inhibiting components, even if both components’ self-diffusion coefficients are equal. Another reason is that reaction-diffusion systems with cross-diffusion can be mathematically ill-posed in several cases, leading to finite-time singularities; see e.g. [33]. At the fundamental level of diffusion processes, the thermodynamic foundation for such non-diagonal diffusion tensors is also problematic, see e.g. [34, 35]. Nevertheless, many reaction-cross-diffusion systems arise as models in applied mathematics, and our goal here is to generalize the notion of Turing conditions for pattern formation to incorporate cross-diffusion. In particular, we want to study when such a system can admit Turing and/or wave instabilities. Within that mathematical modelling setting, we ask how one could design diffusion matrices or linearized reaction kinetics to admit such instabilities. Our objective is to give conditions under which designing unstable systems is possible, alongside particular approaches to doing so.

Specifically, we shall consider either fixing the linearized kinetics of the system and varying the diffusion tensor or fixing the diffusion tensor and varying the linearized kinetics. Assuming stability to homogeneous perturbations (i.e. that the system’s linearized kinetics are stable in the absence of transport), we then ask how to design the remaining free matrix (the diffusion tensor or the linearized kinetics) so that the resulting reaction-diffusion system becomes unstable around its steady state after the addition of transport; that is so that the system undergoes a Turing or a wave instability. In the end, this can be seen as a matter of designing a reaction-diffusion system, subject to constrained transport or constrained kinetics, so that it generates diffusion-driven instabilities under the presence of cross-diffusion. Through examples, we will also explore situations where one does not have complete freedom over either of these matrices and must design the system more carefully. Such questions of design principles are becoming increasingly important both in synthetic biology [36, 37, 38], as well as in materials science and other areas [39, 40]. Previous theoretical work on such design principles has largely focused on reaction-diffusion systems of 2 components [41, 42, 43], so the key novelty in this paper is to consider nn-component reaction-cross-diffusion systems as well as to allow for designing wave instabilities, in addition to Turing instabilities.

1.1 Statement of the main results

For simplicity of presentation, we will focus on reaction-cross-diffusion systems on the real line, hence not being concerned with boundary conditions or geometry, as long as the eigenvalues of the Laplacian on the domain are sufficiently well-behaved. We note that this is essentially without loss of generality in terms of problems posed on Riemannian manifolds with Neumann or periodic boundary conditions; see [14, 8] for discussion of this point in general, and (5, Remark 1) in particular. We do note that the use of Neumann or periodic boundary conditions can have important consequences for wave instabilities as these can give rise to different kinds of patterns, travelling waves or standing waves [5, 44, 45], and that other boundary conditions can induce a variety of behaviours [46, 47]. Given a fixed geometry and boundary conditions, one can simply scale the free matrix discussed below to fit a domain of a particular geometry, in any spatial dimension, assuming the Laplace (or more generally, the Laplace-Beltrami operator) spectrum is known and well-behaved (i.e. consisting solely of point eigenvalues) for the given boundary conditions.

We pose a general reaction-cross-diffusion system as:

∂t𝐮=𝐟⁡(𝐮)+∂x(𝐃⁡(𝐮)​∂x𝐮),\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})+\partial_{x}\left(\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{u})\partial_{x}\mathbf{u}\right), (1)

where 𝐮∈ℝn\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, 𝐟:ℝn→ℝn\mathbf{f}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}, and 𝐃:ℝn→ℝn×ℝn\mathbf{D}:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{n} is the diffusion tensor of the system, which is not necessarily diagonal. We will assume throughout that n≥2n\geq 2, though note that n=2n=2 does not allow for wave instabilities even with cross-diffusion [31]. We assume that sufficiently smooth and unique solutions exist, noting that the existence and regularity theory for these systems is much more intricate than for simpler reaction-diffusion models, with blowup and singularities having a significant literature [48, 49, 50, 51]; see [33] for an introductory review to these complexities and their analysis. We will henceforth neglect details regarding well-posedness and tacitly assume that everything at the nonlinear level is well-behaved.

We assume that Eq. 1 admits a spatially homogeneous steady state 𝐏\mathbf{P} such that 𝐟⁡(𝐏)=𝟎\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{P})=\mathbf{0}, and that 𝐃⁡(𝐏)\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}) has strictly positive real eigenvalues, and hence is invertible for all the values of its argument. After linearizing about this steady state by writing 𝐮=𝐏+ε​𝐮1\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{P}+\varepsilon\mathbf{u}_{1} and keeping terms up to 𝒪⁡(ε)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon), we obtain

∂t𝐮𝟏=𝐉𝐮𝟏+𝐃^​∂x​x𝐮𝟏,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbf{u_{1}}=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{u_{1}}+\mathbf{\hat{D}}\partial_{xx}\mathbf{u_{1}}, (2)

where the constant matrices

𝐃^=𝐃⁡(𝐏),and𝐉=∂𝐮𝐟⁡(𝐏),\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{P}),\qquad\mbox{and}\quad\mathbf{J}=\partial_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{P}),

correspond to diffusion and Jacobian matrices, respectively. Henceforth, we will work with these two constant matrices, dropping the explicit dependence on the steady-state 𝐏\mathbf{P}.

We proceed to solve Eq. 2 in the usual way using separable solutions composed of Laplacian eigenfunctions and solutions in time of the form exp⁡(λ​t)\exp(\lambda t). This leads to solvability conditions determining growth rates λ\lambda as solutions to

det⁡(𝐉−μ​𝐃^−λ​𝐈)=0,\displaystyle\det\left(\mathbf{J}-\mu\mathbf{\hat{D}}-\lambda\mathbf{I}\right)=0, (3)

where μ=k2\mu=k^{2} is an eigenvalue of the negative Laplacian, and kk is a wavenumber. Instabilities of the full system, Eq. 1, correspond to solutions of Eq. 3 with Re(λ)>0\real(\lambda)>0. Henceforth, we will assume that 𝐉\mathbf{J} is a stable matrix; that is, all of its eigenvalues have strictly negative real parts.

In the classical two-species case, we need the Jacobian to have the right sign structure, with two positive and two negative entries [14]. Here, we only assume that it is a non-scalar matrix (i.e. not a scalar multiple of the identity matrix). We then say that the system given by Eq. 2 exhibits a Turing instability if there is at least one purely real value of λ>0\lambda>0 satisfying Eq. 3. Also, we say that the system exhibits a wave instability if there is at least one complex conjugate pair of λ\lambda with positive real part and nontrivial imaginary part satisfying Eq. 3. In both cases, we can then say that the full nonlinear system Eq. 1 exhibits these instabilities around the steady state 𝐏\mathbf{P}.

We now state our main results. We consider ℓ\ell to be a non-negative integer in what comes below.

Theorem 1.

Let 𝐉\mathbf{J} be a non-scalar stable matrix. Then, there exists a diagonalizable diffusion matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} such that Eq. 2 exhibits a Turing instability. Furthermore, if n≥3n\geq 3 and 𝐉\mathbf{J} has at least 1≤ℓ≤31\leq\ell\leq 3 distinct eigenvalues with at least 3−ℓ3-\ell corresponding generalized eigenvectors, then there is also a diagonalizable diffusion matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} such that Eq. 2 exhibits a wave instability.

Theorem 2.

Let 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} be a non-scalar diagonalizable matrix with strictly positive real eigenvalues. Then, there exists a stable matrix 𝐉\mathbf{J} such that Eq. 2 exhibits a Turing instability. Furthermore, if n≥3n\geq 3, then there exists a stable matrix 𝐉\mathbf{J} such that Eq. 2 exhibits a wave instability.

In all of these cases, we give a constructive proof for finding such matrices to induce specific instabilities and provide insights into how to tune parameters to design them to exhibit specific unstable wavelengths. We remark that having matrices inducing these instabilities then allows one to find bifurcation curves where marginal stability is crossed (i.e. where maxμ⁡(Re(λ))=0\max_{\mu}(\real(\lambda))=0 and a transversality condition is satisfied). One can then make use of amplitude equation formalisms to study properties of the solutions near these bifurcation curves [52, 44], and we will explore this in the first example at the end of the paper.

The key idea of the proof for Theorem 1 follows the methods introduced in [5]. That is, by constructing a diagonalizable diffusion tensor, the eigenvalue problem in Eq. 3 is reduced to the analysis of a Jacobian matrix that looks like the ones treated in [5], with the eigenvectors of the diffusion matrix allowing us to effectively control the linearization of the system. We then construct an unstable principal submatrix and set some eigenvalues of the diffusion matrix to zero to ‘pick out’ this submatrix of the (non-scalar) Jacobian matrix, which is guaranteed to destabilize the full system in the limit as μ→∞\mu\to\infty. This effectively allows us to get unstable growth rates λ\lambda with Re(λ)>0\real(\lambda)>0 as μ→∞\mu\to\infty, while all other growth rates will tend to −∞-\infty in this limit. In the end, this gives a way of constructing a suitable matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} so that the linear system exhibits the desired instability.

Next, one introduces a small positive parameter δ\delta that ‘relaxes’ these zero diagonal elements to be small positive numbers and, by continuity, arrives at a system with the correct dispersion relation; that is, there is a finite interval of μ\mu for which Re(λ)>0\real(\lambda)>0, ensuring the desired instability. Turing or wave instabilities can be selected based on the imaginary part of these eigenvalues (chosen via the construction of the unstable principal submatrix above), and the range of μ\mu exhibiting an instability can be tuned arbitrarily (see Lemma 1 and Appendix A). The proof of Theorem 2 is qualitatively similar but proceeds more directly. In particular, we design the Jacobian matrix to ensure the existence of a 22 or 33-component subsystem corresponding to at least two distinct diffusion rates to generate Turing or wave instabilities.

Fig. 1 illustrates the key idea of the constructions for the case of a Turing instability. We construct a principal unstable submatrix that has the largest positive eigenvalue indicated by the green line. When δ=0\delta=0, a dispersion curve of the full system (shown in orange) tends asymptotically to this value as μ→∞\mu\to\infty. We then increase δ\delta to make the diffusion matrix nonsingular. This leads to the blue curves, which have the appropriate form of dispersion relation to ensure a Turing instability with a finite maximally unstable mode. The red curve illustrates the critical value of δ>0\delta>0, which gives this marginal stability criterion such that the dispersion curve is tangent to the horizontal axis. This represents the δ\delta-value at which a Turing bifurcation occurs. The blue dispersion curves thus represent a homotopy between the red and orange curves, parametrized by δ\delta. The proofs below will construct this homotopy explicitly, which will be illustrated in the examples.

Wave instabilities can also be designed similarly. Essentially, we have the same form of dispersion relations as illustrated in Fig. 1, but with each curve now corresponding to the real part of a complex conjugate pair of λ\lambda for each kk. Transitions between Turing and wave instabilities as kk changes can also give rise to more intricate dispersion relations (see, for example, Fig. 5).

Note that the constructions we use for the proofs of Theorem 1 lead to matrices 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} that have strictly positive real-part eigenvalues. However, it should be noted that such matrices may not be symmetric, nor satisfy other functional thermodynamic constraints that are required for a particular application. Similarly, the Jacobian matrix constructed in the proof of Theorem 2 will be of a particular form, which may not satisfy particular physical constraints on the dependent variables. Nevertheless, the constructive proofs we develop are minimal in the sense that they provide exactly the core features of the matrices needed for the instabilities. Thus, in practice, one is left with many free parameters that can be chosen to satisfy additional modelling constraints.

1.2 Outline

The rest of the paper is outlined as follows: Section 2 is devoted to proving Theorem 1 using ideas that largely extend [5]. Section 3 proves Theorem 2 by considering the converse case of freedom in the Jacobian matrix, rather than the diffusion matrix exploited before. We give examples of these theorems, and the particular constructions used to determine the instability-inducing matrices in Section 4, making use of a few additional results on matrix design collected in Appendix A. Finally, Section 5 closes the article with some general remarks and possible extensions of the ideas presented here.

2 Proof of Theorem 1

To prove Theorem 1, we will build some key lemmas extending those in [5] to the case of a cross-diffusion matrix (that is, for 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} being in general non-diagonal). A key step will be to construct a diagonalizable diffusion matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} in order to use previous results applicable only for diagonal diffusion matrices, which we illustrate in the proof of Lemma 1 below. Throughout, we will use subscripts iℓi_{\ell} to denote sequences of positive integer indices. We also define a matrix to be S-stable if all of its principal submatrices are stable. Throughout the paper, the eigenvalues of 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} will be called σi\sigma_{i}, for i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n.

Lemma 1.

Let 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} be diagonalizable matrix; specifically, there exists a non-singular matrix 𝐐\mathbf{Q} such that 𝔻:=𝐐−1​𝐃^​𝐐\mathbb{D}:=\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{\hat{D}}\mathbf{Q} is a diagonal matrix. Suppose further that 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} has ℓ\ell eigenvalues σi1,…,σiℓ\sigma_{i_{1}},\ldots,\sigma_{i_{\ell}} equal to zero, while all others are positive. Then, there exist ℓ\ell eigenvalues of 𝐉−μ​𝐃^\mathbf{J}-\mu\mathbf{\hat{D}} that tend to the eigenvalues of the principal submatrix of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} that comprises its i1th,…,iℓthi_{1}^{\rm th},\ldots,i_{\ell}^{\rm th} rows and columns as μ→∞\mu\to\infty. Meanwhile, the real parts of the eigenvalues associated with the principal submatrix of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} that excludes these rows and columns all tend to −∞-\infty as μ→∞\mu\to\infty.

Proof.

First, if ℓ=n\ell=n, then all the eigenvalues of 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} are equal to zero. Therefore, as 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} is diagonalizable, this implies it must be equal to the zero matrix, entailing that the eigenvalues of 𝐉−μ​𝐃^\mathbf{J}-\mu\mathbf{\hat{D}} are equal to the eigenvalues of 𝐉\mathbf{J} for every μ>0\mu>0, which proves the result in this case.

On the other hand, if 1≤ℓ<n1\leq\ell<n, we have that the eigenvalues λm\lambda_{m} of 𝐉−μ​𝐃^\mathbf{J}-\mu\mathbf{\hat{D}} are determined by:

𝐉𝐯m−μ​𝐃^​𝐯m−λm​𝐯m=0,\displaystyle\mathbf{J}\mathbf{v}_{m}-\mu\mathbf{\hat{D}}\mathbf{v}_{m}-\lambda_{m}\mathbf{v}_{m}=0,

where 𝐯m\mathbf{v}_{m} is a corresponding eigenvector for each m=1,…,nm=1,\ldots,n. Now, using that 𝐃^=𝐐​𝔻​𝐐−1\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbb{D}\mathbf{Q}^{-1}, we know that this equation is equivalent to

𝐉𝐯m−μ​𝐐​𝔻​𝐐−1​𝐯m=λm​𝐯m,\displaystyle\mathbf{J}\mathbf{v}_{m}-\mu\mathbf{Q}\mathbb{D}\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{v}_{m}=\lambda_{m}\mathbf{v}_{m},

which implies

𝐐−1​𝐉𝐯m−μ​𝔻​𝐐−1​𝐯m=λm​𝐐−1​𝐯m.\displaystyle\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{v}_{m}-\mu\mathbb{D}\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{v}_{m}=\lambda_{m}\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{v}_{m}. (4)

Let 𝐰m=𝐐−1​𝐯m\mathbf{w}_{m}=\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{v}_{m}. Therefore, Eq. 4 becomes

𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐𝐰m−μ​𝔻​𝐰m=λm​𝐰m,\displaystyle\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{w}_{m}-\mu\mathbb{D}\mathbf{w}_{m}=\lambda_{m}\mathbf{w}_{m}, (5)

which is equivalent to the linearization of the general system analyzed in [5], for 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} instead of 𝐉\mathbf{J}. This implies that (5, Lemma 5) can be used to conclude the proof. ∎

To use the lemma above, we are going to focus on proving the existence of stable matrices 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} with unstable principal submatrices to conclude that the system can exhibit different diffusion-driven instabilities. Lemma 1 tells us that, to construct the diffusion matrices that allow the appearance of these instabilities, we need to follow two steps: first, we find the matrix 𝐐\mathbf{Q} of eigenvectors of 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} such that 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} has an unstable principal submatrix; second, we change the eigenvalues of 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} in order to control the convergence of the eigenvalues of 𝐉−μ​𝐃^\mathbf{J}-\mu\mathbf{\hat{D}} as μ→∞\mu\to\infty (i.e. set the corresponding eigenvalues to asymptotically small values to induce the instability). While the case of zero diffusion coefficients corresponding to this principal unstable submatrix will lead to an ill-posed linear system, we can fix this by simply using small positive values instead of zeroes; see Fig. 1 for an illustration. An important point here is to understand what kind of structure we want to have for the unstable principle submatrix, and then use this structure to design the eigenvectors 𝐐\mathbf{Q} of the diffusion matrix to ensure that this submatrix appears within 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q}.

To continue, it is useful to recall a standard result from linear algebra: if two matrices 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B} have the same Jordan normal form, then 𝐀\mathbf{A} and 𝐁\mathbf{B} are similar. That is, there exists a non-singular matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R} such that 𝐀=𝐑𝐁𝐑−1\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{R}^{-1} [53]. Furthermore, we recall that if 𝐀\mathbf{A} is a diagonalizable matrix of size n×nn\times n, then 𝐀\mathbf{A} has only one eigenvalue (with algebraic multiplicity nn) if and only if 𝐀\mathbf{A} is a scalar matrix (i.e. a scalar multiple of the identity). We make use of the following procedure to reduce similarity in general to the question of similarity of principal submatrices arising from Jordan normal forms. We will also use the notation 𝐈ℓ\mathbf{I_{\ell}} to stand for the ℓ\ell by ℓ\ell identity matrix, and 𝟎𝐢,𝐣\mathbf{0_{i,j}} for an i×ji\times j block of zeros. In both cases, these matrices are omitted when any of their sizes is lower than one (i.e. if 𝐈ℓ\mathbf{I_{\ell}} appears in an expression, and ℓ≤0\ell\leq 0, then the matrix is omitted).

Remark 1.

Let 𝐉\mathbf{J} be similar to a matrix with ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 square blocks given by

𝐂=diag​(𝐂𝟏,…,𝐂ℓ).\displaystyle\mathbf{C}=\mbox{diag}\left(\mathbf{C_{1}},\ldots,\mathbf{C_{\ell}}\right).

Let us assume that there exists 1≤j≤ℓ1\leq j\leq\ell such that 𝐂𝐣\mathbf{C_{j}} is similar to 𝐊\mathbf{K}, with 𝐊\mathbf{K} being a square matrix of the same size as 𝐂𝐣\mathbf{C_{j}}. This implies that there exists an invertible matrix 𝐑\mathbf{R} such that 𝐂𝐣​𝐑=𝐑𝐊\mathbf{C_{j}}\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{K}. Therefore, if we define 𝐐=diag​(𝐈𝟏,…,𝐈𝐣−𝟏,𝐑,𝐈𝐣+𝟏,…,𝐈ℓ)\mathbf{Q}=\mbox{diag}\left(\mathbf{I_{1}},\ldots,\mathbf{I_{j-1}},\mathbf{R},\mathbf{I_{j+1}},\ldots,\mathbf{I_{\ell}}\right), then we note that

𝐂𝐐=𝐐𝐌,\displaystyle\mathbf{C}\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{M},

where

𝐌=diag​(𝐂𝟏,…,𝐂𝐣−𝟏,𝐊,𝐂𝐣+𝟏,…,𝐂ℓ),\displaystyle\mathbf{M}=\mbox{diag}\left(\mathbf{C_{1}},\ldots,\mathbf{C_{j-1}},\mathbf{K},\mathbf{C_{j+1}},\ldots,\mathbf{C_{\ell}}\right),

implying that we can construct similar matrices only by establishing similarities of square blocks in the diagonal of the Jordan matrix of 𝐉\mathbf{J}.

We now give a constructive proof for Theorem 1. The idea of the proof is to find a matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} that ensures that the system exhibits either Turing or wave instabilities. In Lemma 1, we show that the existence of an unstable principal submatrix is a sufficient criterion to ensure the appearance of any kind of linear instability. The proof will proceed then, for each kind of instability, by constructing a matrix 𝐊\mathbf{K} similar to 𝐉\mathbf{J} with an unstable principal submatrix. In each case, we proceed by directly writing down a matrix 𝐊\mathbf{K} with the right unstable submatrix for a particular kind of instability and then showing that this can be made similar to 𝐉\mathbf{J} through the correct choice of 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}}. Note throughout that there will be several free parameters at the end of the construction, leaving freedom one could exploit to match any further constraints arising from the modelling context.

2.1 Turing instabilities

We start by providing the following result for 2-component systems.

Lemma 2.

Let n=2n=2, and 𝐉\mathbf{J} be a non-scalar stable matrix. Then, there exists a diffusion matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} so that Eq. 2 exhibits a Turing instability.

Proof.

Let us denote the elements of 𝐉\mathbf{J} by

𝐉=(abcd).\displaystyle\mathbf{J}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}.

Consider the following matrix:

𝐊\displaystyle\mathbf{K} =(a+d−1a​d−b​c−a−d+1−11),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}a+d-1&&a\,d-b\,c-a-d+1\\ -1&&1\end{pmatrix},

which clearly fulfills tr⁡(𝐊)=tr⁡(𝐉)\tr(\m{K})=\tr\left(\mathbf{J}\right) and det⁡(𝐊)=det⁡(𝐉)\det(\m{K})=\det\left(\mathbf{J}\right), implying that both matrices have the same eigenvalues.

We now prove that these matrices are similar. In fact, consider

𝐐=(α(d−1)​α−b​γγ(a−1)​γ−c​α),\displaystyle\mathbf{Q}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&&(d-1)\,\alpha-b\,\gamma\\ \gamma&&(a-1)\,\gamma-c\,\alpha\end{pmatrix},

for α,γ∈ℝ\alpha,\gamma\in\mathbb{R}. It is easy to see that

𝐉𝐐\displaystyle\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} =𝐐𝐊,\displaystyle=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{K},

and

det⁡(𝐐)=b​γ2+(a−d)​α​γ−c​α2,\displaystyle\det(\m{Q})=b\,\gamma^{2}+(a-d)\,\alpha\,\gamma-c\,\alpha^{2},

which is either a quadratic or a linear function on α\alpha or γ\gamma, as a≠da\neq d, b≠0b\neq 0 or c≠0c\neq 0. This is true since, as 𝐉\mathbf{J} is not a scalar matrix, then the elements in the diagonal must not be equal or the off-diagonal terms must not be zero at the same time. We can then take any pair (α,γ)(\alpha,\gamma) so that det⁡(𝐐)≠0\det(\m{Q})\neq 0.

This proves that 𝐉\mathbf{J} is similar to 𝐊\mathbf{K}, which is a stable matrix with an unstable principal submatrix. Therefore, by choosing a suitable diagonal matrix 𝔻\mathbb{D}, we can construct the matrix 𝐃^=𝐐​𝔻​𝐐−1\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbb{D}\mathbf{Q}^{-1} so that the result holds by using Lemma 1 (i.e. by choosing a sufficiently small bottom-right diagonal element to ensure a positive λ\lambda for some μ>0\mu>0, thanks to the positive bottom-right element of 𝐊\mathbf{K}). ∎

Using Remark 1, and the fact that any non-scalar matrix 𝐉\mathbf{J} will have a 2×22\times 2 non-scalar block in its Jordan Normal Form, we can immediately use Lemma 2 to construct a suitable matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} to induce Turing instabilities. The similarity matrix 𝐐\mathbf{Q} constructed in the proof of the Lemma is the key to proving the general result. Note that 𝐊\mathbf{K} was chosen in order to fulfill the conditions provided in Lemma 1, but there are infinitely many other matrices that are similar to 𝐉\mathbf{J} and have an unstable principal submatrix.

2.2 Wave instabilities

We will now use similar constructions to demonstrate how to achieve wave instabilities with suitable choices of 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}}.

Lemma 3.

Let 𝐉\mathbf{J} be a non-scalar stable matrix and n=3n=3 or n=4n=4. If 𝐉\mathbf{J} has 1≤ℓ≤31\leq\ell\leq 3 distinct eigenvalues, then there exists a diffusion matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} so that Eq. 2 exhibits a wave instability provided 𝐉\mathbf{J} has at least 3−ℓ3-\ell generalized eigenvectors.

Proof.

We first consider the case n=3n=3. Let us denote the elements of 𝐉\mathbf{J} by

𝐉=(abcdefghi).\displaystyle\mathbf{J}=\begin{pmatrix}a&b&c\\ d&e&f\\ g&h&i\end{pmatrix}.

Consider the following matrix

𝐊=(ℓ1,1ℓ1,2ℓ1,3α1−1γ11),\displaystyle\mathbf{K}=\begin{pmatrix}\ell_{1,1}&\ell_{1,2}&\ell_{1,3}\\ \alpha&1&-1\\ \gamma&1&1\end{pmatrix},

where α,γ∈ℝ\alpha,\gamma\in\mathbb{R}, and

ℓ1,1\displaystyle\ell_{1,1} =a+e+i−2,\displaystyle=a+e+i-2,
ℓ1,2\displaystyle\ell_{1,2} =2​α​(a+e+i−1)−2​γ+(M12+M13+M23)​(γ−α)−γ​det⁡(𝐉)α2+γ2,\displaystyle=\frac{2\alpha(a+e+i-1)-2\gamma+\left(M_{12}+M_{13}+M_{23}\right)(\gamma-\alpha)-\gamma\det(\jac)}{\alpha^{2}+\gamma^{2}},
ℓ1,3\displaystyle\ell_{1,3} =2​(γ⁡(a+e+i−1)+α)−(M12+M13+M23)​(α+γ)+α​det⁡(𝐉)α2+γ2,\displaystyle=\frac{2(\gamma(a+e+i-1)+\alpha)-\left(M_{12}+M_{13}+M_{23}\right)(\alpha+\gamma)+\alpha\det(\jac)}{\alpha^{2}+\gamma^{2}},

with

M12=a​e−b​d,M13=a​i−c​g,M23=e​i−f​h.\displaystyle M_{12}=ae-bd,\qquad M_{13}=ai-cg,\qquad M_{23}=ei-fh.

Note that ℓ1,2\ell_{1,2} and ℓ1,3\ell_{1,3} are well-defined provided that α2+γ2≠0\alpha^{2}+\gamma^{2}\neq 0.

Now, we consider the case when 𝐉\mathbf{J} has three distinct eigenvalues. By construction, we have that the characteristic polynomials of 𝐉\mathbf{J} and 𝐊\mathbf{K} are the same, which implies that these matrices are similar (enforcing this similarity is precisely how the ℓ1,i\ell_{1,i} were constructed). We highlight that the 2×22\times 2 submatrix at the bottom right corner of 𝐊\mathbf{K} has eigenvalues 1±i1\pm i. Therefore, by arguments similar to those used at the end of the proof of Lemma 2, we can construct a matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} to conclude the first part of the proof using the result in Lemma 1.

On the other hand, if 𝐉\mathbf{J} has repeated eigenvalues, then all of them must be real (as any complex eigenvalue of a real matrix comes in pairs). This implies that 𝐉\mathbf{J} is similar to one of the matrices below:

𝐂𝟏=(−y000−zℓ00−z),𝐂𝟐=(−zℓ200−zℓ100−z)\displaystyle\mathbf{C_{1}}=\begin{pmatrix}-y&0&0\\ 0&-z&\ell\\ 0&0&-z\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf{C_{2}}=\begin{pmatrix}-z&\ell_{2}&0\\ 0&-z&\ell_{1}\\ 0&0&-z\end{pmatrix}

where y,z>0y,z>0 are real numbers so that y≠zy\neq z, and ℓ,ℓ1,ℓ2∈{0,1}\ell,\ell_{1},\ell_{2}\in\{0,1\}. which is different from zero as long as ℓ1​ℓ2​r3,1≠0\ell_{1}\ell_{2}r_{3,1}\neq 0 and α2+γ2≠0\alpha^{2}+\gamma^{2}\neq 0, which implies that ℓ1=ℓ2=1\ell_{1}=\ell_{2}=1. Again, see Appendix B where we show that such an 𝐑\mathbf{R} can always be found. In the case n=4n=4, we can use Remark 1 to reduce this to a 3×33\times 3 block of the Jordan normal form of 𝐉\mathbf{J}, unless 𝐉\mathbf{J} has repeated complex conjugate eigenvalues (note that a repeated real root and a complex-conjugate pair can be subsumed in the case of 3 distinct eigenvalues). The only case not covered by the arguments above then, is if there is a repeated complex-conjugate pair of eigenvalues. In this case, we consider

𝐊=(ℓ1,1ℓ1,2ℓ1,3ℓ1,4γα00δ0−ααε0−α−α),and𝐂𝟑=(α−βℓ0βα0ℓ00α−β00βα),\displaystyle\mathbf{K}=\begin{pmatrix}\ell_{1,1}&\ell_{1,2}&\ell_{1,3}&\ell_{1,4}\\ \gamma&\alpha&0&0\\ \delta&0&-\alpha&\alpha\\ \varepsilon&0&-\alpha&-\alpha\end{pmatrix},\qquad\text{and}\quad\qquad\mathbf{C_{3}}=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&-\beta&\ell&0\\ \beta&\alpha&0&\ell\\ 0&0&\alpha&-\beta\\ 0&0&\beta&\alpha\end{pmatrix},

where α<0\alpha<0, and β>0\beta>0 are real numbers and ℓ∈{0,1}\ell\in\{0,1\}. In this case, we note (via direct calculation) that the characteristic polynomials of 𝐊\mathbf{K} and 𝐂𝟑\mathbf{C_{3}} are equal if

ℓ1,1\displaystyle\ell_{1,1} =5​α,\displaystyle=5\alpha,
ℓ1,2\displaystyle\ell_{1,2} =−β45​α2​γ,\displaystyle=-\frac{\beta^{4}}{5\alpha^{2}\gamma},

This implies that we have the constraints γ≠0\gamma\neq 0 and δ2+ε2≠0\delta^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}\neq 0 in order to be able to make these matrices similar. So, as before, we note that 𝐊\mathbf{K} will be similar to 𝐂𝟑\mathbf{C_{3}} if there exists a matrix 𝐑=(ri,j)i,j\mathbf{R}=\left(r_{i,j}\right)_{i,j} such that 𝐂𝟑​𝐑=𝐑𝐊\mathbf{C_{3}}\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{R}\mathbf{K}. In this case, if we leave r1,1,r2,1r_{1,1},r_{2,1}, r3,1r_{3,1} and r4,1r_{4,1} as parameters of the solution (and solve for the other 1212 elements of 𝐑\mathbf{R}), then the determinant of 𝐑\mathbf{R} will be given by

−4​β4​ℓ2​(r3,12+r4,12)25​α3​γ​(δ2+ε2),\displaystyle-\frac{4\beta^{4}\ell^{2}\left(r_{3,1}^{2}+r_{4,1}^{2}\right)^{2}}{5\alpha^{3}\gamma\left(\delta^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}\right)},

which is different from zero provided that ℓ=1\ell=1, and r3,12+r4,12≠0r_{3,1}^{2}+r_{4,1}^{2}\neq 0. Note that the 2×22\times 2 bottom-right submatrix of 𝐊\mathbf{K} has eigenvalues −α±α​i-\alpha\pm\alpha i, which have a positive real part, as α<0\alpha<0. As before, we can therefore construct a matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} to conclude the proof using the result in Lemma 1.

Once again, we can conclude that a wave instability can be generated when n=4n=4 and 𝐉\mathbf{J} has only two distinct complex-conjugate eigenvalues as long as it has two generalized eigenvectors.

∎

We remark that the case n=3n=3 is minimal except that it does not account for repeated complex-conjugate eigenvalues, hence why we included the case n=4n=4 in the statement of the previous lemma. We also note that other matrices 𝐊\mathbf{K} can be chosen to arrive at similar results via different constructions. For instance, in the n=4n=4 case above, the entries or the location of the principal submatrix at the bottom right corner of 𝐊\mathbf{K} does not change the result, and the elements of the second row and column of the 4×44\times 4 matrix 𝐊\mathbf{K} can also be non-zero and the result will be the same (with a suitable modification of 𝐑\mathbf{R} and 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}}).

With this, we are ready to prove the first main result of this article.

Proof of Theorem 1.

First, we consider how to induce Turing instabilities. Given that 𝐉\mathbf{J} is non-scalar, we know there must exist a non-scalar 2×22\times 2 sub-block of its Jordan normal form which is also non-scalar. We can apply Lemma 2 to find a matrix 𝐊\mathbf{K} similar to this sub-block, and by construction, this 𝐊\mathbf{K} will have a principle unstable submatrix that induces a Turing instability. We then use the construction given in Remark 1 to embed this similarity inside of the matrix 𝐌\mathbf{M} in that remark, and then apply Lemma 1 on the matrix 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q}, which now has a principal unstable submatrix by construction. This Lemma allows us to set one of the eigenvalues of the diffusion matrix (i.e. an element of 𝔻\mathbb{D}) to zero in order to excite the corresponding unstable principal submatrix and induce a Turing instability in the full system. Note that we can take all other elements of 𝔻\mathbb{D} as any arbitrary positive numbers in order to use Lemma 1.

The proof for inducing wave instabilities proceeds in an analogous way as above, except that we will make use of Lemma 3 to construct a matrix 𝐊\mathbf{K} similar to 𝐉\mathbf{J}, instead. By assumption, 𝐉\mathbf{J} has 1≤ℓ≤31\leq\ell\leq 3 distinct eigenvalues with at least 3−ℓ3-\ell corresponding generalised eigenvectors. Hence, either 𝐉\mathbf{J} has a 3×33\times 3 sub-block of its Jordan normal form that exactly fulfills this criterion as well, or it has a 4×44\times 4 sub-block with two repeated complex conjugate eigenvalues. In either of these cases, we can again embed the appropriate matrix 𝐊\mathbf{K} from the proof of Lemma 3 into the matrix 𝐌\mathbf{M} from above in order to construct a suitable similarity matrix 𝐐\mathbf{Q} such that 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} has a principal unstable submatrix with complex-conjugate unstable eigenvalues. Again, through an analogous use of Lemma 1, we can set the appropriate two elements of 𝔻\mathbb{D} to zero to induce a wave instability in the full system. This concludes the proof.

∎

We remark that, in practice, one needs the zero elements of 𝔻\mathbb{D} to be asymptotically small rather than strictly zero to avoid ill-posedness of the linear problem, but the existence of the instability will persist for some range of ‘small’ diffusion constants. We note that in both the diagonal matrices 𝔻\mathbb{D} and in the similarity matrices 𝐐\mathbf{Q} constructed above, one has, in principle, freedom over elements not affecting the principal unstable submatrix to use more general constructions to gain additional flexibility over the elements we have not exploited here. We will illustrate some aspects of this in Appendix A through alternative lemmas one can use to construct these matrices, and in the examples in Section 4.

3 Proof of Theorem 2

As in the previous section, we prove Theorem 2 by dividing it into cases, though as the eigenvalues of 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} are all real, the number of sub-cases we need to consider is fewer than in the proof of Theorem 1.

We assume, without loss of generality, that the eigenvalues of 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} (i.e. the elements of 𝔻\mathbb{D}) are sorted in ascending order so that 0<σi≤σi+10<\sigma_{i}\leq\sigma_{i+1} for all i=1,…,n−1i=1,\ldots,n-1.

3.1 Turing instabilities

Lemma 4.

Let n≥2n\geq 2 and 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} be a non-scalar diagonalizable matrix with real and strictly positive eigenvalues. Then, there exists a stable matrix 𝐉\mathbf{J} such that Eq. 2 exhibits a Turing instability.

Proof.

As 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} is a diagonalizable non-scalar matrix with positive real eigenvalues and the elements of its diagonalization 𝔻\mathbb{D} are sorted, then there must exist at least one integer 1≤ℓ≤n−11\leq\ell\leq n-1 such that σℓ<σℓ+1\sigma_{\ell}<\sigma_{\ell+1}.

Therefore, as the eigenvalues of 𝐉−μ​𝐃^\mathbf{J}-\mu\mathbf{\hat{D}} are the same as the ones of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐−μ​𝔻\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q}-\mu\mathbb{D}, we consider

𝐉=𝐐𝐂𝐐−1,\displaystyle\mathbf{J}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{Q}^{-1},

where

𝐂=(−𝐈ℓ−𝟏𝟎ℓ−𝟏,𝟐𝟎ℓ−𝟏,𝐧−ℓ−𝟏𝟎𝟐,ℓ−𝟏𝐒∗𝟎𝟐,𝐧−ℓ−𝟏𝟎𝐧−ℓ−𝟏,ℓ−𝟏𝟎𝐧−ℓ−𝟏,𝟐−𝐈𝐧−ℓ−𝟏),\displaystyle\mathbf{C}=\begin{pmatrix}-\mathbf{I_{\ell-1}}&\mathbf{0_{\ell-1,2}}&\mathbf{0_{\ell-1,n-\ell-1}}\\ \mathbf{0_{2,\ell-1}}&\mathbf{S^{*}}&\mathbf{0_{2,n-\ell-1}}\\ \mathbf{0_{n-\ell-1,\ell-1}}&\mathbf{0_{n-\ell-1,2}}&-\mathbf{I_{n-\ell-1}}\end{pmatrix},

with

𝐒∗=(bb⁡(b+c)+q−1−(b+c)),\displaystyle\mathbf{S^{*}}=\begin{pmatrix}b&b(b+c)+q\\ -1&-(b+c)\end{pmatrix},

and b,c,q>0b,c,q>0 are real constants to be determined. By checking its trace and determinant, one can see that 𝐒∗\mathbf{S^{*}} is stable. By construction, we have that n−2n-2 eigenvalues of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐−μ​𝔻\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q}-\mu\mathbb{D} have the form −1−σi-1-\sigma_{i}, for a corresponding integer 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n such that i≠ℓ,ℓ+1i\neq\ell,\ell+1. On the other hand, by considering the two eigenvalues we have singled out via 𝐒∗\mathbf{S^{*}}, we see that the equations that determine them are uncoupled from all others and, hence, they form an n=2n=2 linear system which is precisely the classical Turing system, with 𝐒∗\mathbf{S^{*}} playing the role of the 2×22\times 2 Jacobian matrix. Thus, the largest of the other two eigenvalues will be positive for some value of μ>0\mu>0 if the system satisfies the classical 2-component Turing conditions (see, e.g., [14]):

σℓ+1​b−σℓ​(b+c)\displaystyle\sigma_{\ell+1}b-\sigma_{\ell}(b+c) >0,and\displaystyle>0,\quad\text{and}
(σℓ+1​b−σℓ​(b+c))2\displaystyle\left(\sigma_{\ell+1}b-\sigma_{\ell}(b+c)\right)^{2} >4​σℓ​σℓ+1​q,\displaystyle>4\sigma_{\ell}\sigma_{\ell+1}q,

which hold provided that

b>σℓ​cσℓ+1−σℓ>0\displaystyle b>\frac{\sigma_{\ell}c}{\sigma_{\ell+1}-\sigma_{\ell}}>0

and

q<(σℓ+1​b−σℓ​(b+c))24​σℓ​σℓ+1.\displaystyle q<\frac{\left(\sigma_{\ell+1}b-\sigma_{\ell}(b+c)\right)^{2}}{4\sigma_{\ell}\sigma_{\ell+1}}.

Hence, we can always pick values of b,c,b,c, and qq to satisfy these, given any pair of distinct eigenvalues σℓ<σℓ+1\sigma_{\ell}<\sigma_{\ell+1}. Therefore, if we set 𝐉\mathbf{J} using this construction, we will induce a Turing instability in the original system given by Eq. 2. ∎

3.2 Wave instabilities

We next prove an analogous result to the previous lemma for the case of wave instabilities. Due to these requiring a 3-component subsystem, the constructions are a bit more involved.

Lemma 5.

Let n≥3n\geq 3 and 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} be a non-scalar diagonalizable matrix with real and strictly positive eigenvalues. Then, there exists a stable matrix 𝐉\mathbf{J} such that the full system exhibits a wave instability.

Proof.

As 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} is a non-scalar diagonalizable matrix with positive real eigenvalues and the elements in 𝔻\mathbb{D} are sorted, then there must exist at least one integer 1≤ℓ≤n−21\leq\ell\leq n-2 such that σℓ<σℓ+2\sigma_{\ell}<\sigma_{\ell+2}.

Let us consider 𝐉=𝐐𝐂𝐐−1\mathbf{J}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{C}\mathbf{Q}^{-1}, where

𝐂=(−𝐈ℓ−𝟏𝟎ℓ−𝟏,𝟑𝟎ℓ−𝟏,𝐧−ℓ−𝟐𝟎𝟑,ℓ−𝟏𝐒∗𝟎𝟑,𝐧−ℓ−𝟐𝟎𝐧−ℓ−𝟐,ℓ−𝟏𝟎𝐧−ℓ−𝟐,𝟑−𝐈𝐧−ℓ−𝟐),\displaystyle\mathbf{C}=\begin{pmatrix}-\mathbf{I_{\ell-1}}&\mathbf{0_{\ell-1,3}}&\mathbf{0_{\ell-1,n-\ell-2}}\\ \mathbf{0_{3,\ell-1}}&\mathbf{S^{*}}&\mathbf{0_{3,n-\ell-2}}\\ \mathbf{0_{n-\ell-2,\ell-1}}&\mathbf{0_{n-\ell-2,3}}&-\mathbf{I_{n-\ell-2}}\end{pmatrix},

with

𝐒∗=(b−bc​y−b⁡(2​b+c)bbb​c+y⁡(2​b+c)+z1−1−(2​b+c)),\displaystyle\mathbf{S^{*}}=\begin{pmatrix}b&-b&cy-b(2b+c)\\ b&b&bc+y(2b+c)+z\\ 1&-1&-(2b+c)\end{pmatrix},

and b,c,y,z>0b,c,y,z>0 are real parameters to be determined. Note that tr⁡(𝐒∗)=−c<0\tr{\m{S^*}}=-c<0. Furthermore, the eigenvalues of the 2×22\times 2 submatrix at the top left corner of 𝐒∗\mathbf{S^{*}} are given by b±b​ib\pm bi. We also note that 𝐒∗\mathbf{S^{*}} is a stable matrix, as its characteristic polynomial for an eigenvalue η\eta is given by

η3+c​η2+(2​b​y+z)​η+2​b​c​y=0,\eta^{3}+c\eta^{2}+\left(2by+z\right)\eta+2bcy=0,

which satisfies the Routh-Hurwitz stability conditions.

Now, when we consider the full system, we note that (by the construction of 𝐂\mathbf{C}) n−3n-3 eigenvalues of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐−μ​𝔻\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q}-\mu\mathbb{D} have the form −1−σi-1-\sigma_{i}, for a corresponding integer 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n such that i≠ℓ,ℓ+1,ℓ+2i\neq\ell,\ell+1,\ell+2. Moreover, the other three eigenvalues are solutions to the following equation:

Remark 2.

While the above lemma uses a specific form of a Jacobian matrix, in principle one can construct a stable matrix of a different form by putting another unstable submatrix at the top left corner of 𝐒∗\mathbf{S^{*}} by then making sure one ensures the existence of zeroes of Eq. 10 for some positive values of μ\mu. Even with the form of the Jacobian block used, one can freely vary cc, qq, and zz, needing to only ensure that bb is sufficiently large. One can compute an explicit minimum value for bb, but it is somewhat tedious and easier to check that bb is sufficiently large by directly computing the dispersion relation (i.e. plotting Re(λ⁡(μ))\real(\lambda(\mu))).

Proof of Theorem 2.

The proof is analogous to the proof of Theorem 1, though simpler as we can directly use Lemmas 4 and 5 to design unstable submatrices of 𝐉\mathbf{J} fulfilling the criteria for each kind of instability. ∎

We remark that, as long as one ensures that 𝐉\mathbf{J} is a stable matrix, there is otherwise freedom to design all other nonzero elements of the matrix away from those that ensure these specific unstable submatrices. With more effort, one can modify other elements of 𝐉\mathbf{J}, but will need to use more general constructions than those proposed here.

4 Examples

We now employ the constructions used in the proofs of the main theorems, as well as some additional results collected in Appendix A to illustrate the design of Turing and wave instabilities in a handful of prototypical reaction-cross-diffusion systems. The examples here demonstrate the key ingredients needed to use the results and how the freedom in the constructions allows one to satisfy additional constraints and still achieve the correct instabilities.

We denote 𝐒𝐢𝟏​…​𝐢ℓ\mathbf{S_{i_{1}\ldots i_{\ell}}} the principle submatrix of 𝐉\mathbf{J} composed of the rows and columns with labels i1,…,iℓi_{1},\ldots,i_{\ell}, where 1≤i1<…<iℓ≤n1\leq i_{1}<\ldots<i_{\ell}\leq n is a set of non-repeated integers. We will plot dispersion relations (i.e. Re(λ⁡(μ))\real(\lambda(\mu))) with continuous (respectively, dashed) lines representing purely real (respectively, complex non-real) eigenvalues. In other words, we will not plot the imaginary parts of λ⁡(μ)\lambda(\mu) but instead use a dashed line for a given value of μ\mu to indicate a complex growth rate λ\lambda, showing only its real part.

We compute direct numerical solutions of the PDE models implemented using finite differences in space with the 3-point (1D) and 5-point (2D) standard Laplace stencil (or a suitable centred-difference approach for the case of a nonlinear diffusion coefficient), and then integrate in time using the Matlab function ode15s, which implements backwards differentiation formulae of orders 1 to 5. We used relative and absolute tolerances of 10−910^{-9} and also checked numerical convergence in decreasing spatial step sizes for some specific simulations. In 1D (respectively, 2D) simulations, we used 1,0001,000 (respectively, 200×200200\times 200) discrete nodes. Throughout, we use initial data of the form 𝐮|t=0=𝐏+η𝒩(0,1)\mathbf{u}\rvert_{t=0}=\mathbf{P}+\eta\mathcal{N}(0,1), which are small normally-distributed random perturbations of the initial condition with variance η\eta. In all simulations, we used η=0.01\eta=0.01. All of the codes used for time integration can be found on GitHub22 2 https://github.com/AndrewLKrause/Designing-reaction-cross-diffusion-systems, and there we also include four links to interactive web-based versions of the simulations using VisualPDE [55].

4.1 3-component Schnakenberg system

The Schnakenberg system was intended to be a simple 2-component model for glycolysis exhibiting limit cycles [56, 4, 57], and is well-studied in pattern formation largely because of its simplistic form and presentation in the textbook [14]. Here, in order to exhibit wave instabilities, we consider a simple 3-component extension obtained after adding a third variable to the classical model as in [58]. However, we also include linear cross-diffusion terms not accounted for there. The reaction-diffusion system is given by

∂t𝐮=𝐟⁡(𝐮)+𝐃^​∂x​x𝐮,\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})+\mathbf{\hat{D}}\partial_{xx}\mathbf{u}, (11)

where

𝐮\displaystyle\mathbf{u} =(u,v,w)⊺,𝐟(𝐮)=(a−u+u2​vb−u2​vu−w),and𝐃^=(D1,1D1,2D1,3D2,1D2,2D2,3D3,1D3,2D3,3).\displaystyle=(u,v,w)^{\intercal},\quad\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})=\begin{pmatrix}a-u+u^{2}v\\ b-u^{2}v\\ u-w\end{pmatrix},\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\begin{pmatrix}D_{1,1}&D_{1,2}&D_{1,3}\\ D_{2,1}&D_{2,2}&D_{2,3}\\ D_{3,1}&D_{3,2}&D_{3,3}\end{pmatrix}.

This system has only one homogeneous steady state given by

𝐏=(u∗,v∗,w∗)=(a+b,b(a+b)2,a+b).\displaystyle\mathbf{P}=\left(u^{*},v^{*},w^{*}\right)=\left(a+b,\frac{b}{(a+b)^{2}},a+b\right).

In this example, we will assume that we can vary the diffusion matrix to obtain wave instabilities, without any further constraints. Hence, we will be using ideas from the proof of Theorem 1, which are presented in Section 2. To be concrete, consider the parameter values (a,b)=(1,1/2)(a,b)=(1,1/2). The Jacobian matrix of the system at 𝐏\mathbf{P} is then

𝐉=(−13940−23−94010−1),\displaystyle\mathbf{J}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}-\frac{1}{3}&\frac{9}{4}&0\\[4.30554pt] -\frac{2}{3}&-\frac{9}{4}&0\\[4.30554pt] 1&0&-1\end{array}\right),

which has eigenvalues −1-1 and 124​(−31±335​i)\frac{1}{24}\left(-31\pm\sqrt{335}i\right). Table 1 shows the eigenvalues of the principal submatrices of 𝐉\mathbf{J}.

The Jacobian matrix and all of its principal submatrices are stable. This means that a diagonal diffusion matrix is unable to produce diffusion-driven instabilities [21, 5]. However, we can find a cross-diffusion matrix so that the system exhibits wave instabilities. As detailed in the proof of Lemma 3, we can choose an unstable 2×22\times 2 matrix with two unstable eigenvalues to find a suitable diffusion matrix that destabilizes the system.

In particular, we note that 𝐉\mathbf{J} has three different eigenvalues, so we can find parameters α,γ,ℓ1,ℓ2,ℓ3∈ℝ\alpha,\gamma,\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ell_{3}\in\mathbb{R} so that 𝐉\mathbf{J} is similar to

𝐂=(197α1ℓ1ℓ2ℓ3−39072γ−235312).\displaystyle\mathbf{C}=\begin{pmatrix}197&\alpha&1\\ \ell_{1}&\ell_{2}&\ell_{3}\\ -39072&\gamma&-\frac{2353}{12}\end{pmatrix}.

We choose α=0\alpha=0 and γ=94\gamma=\frac{9}{4} and note that these two matrices are similar if and only if

ℓ1=38940,ℓ2=−92,ℓ3=11596.\displaystyle\ell_{1}=38940,\qquad\ell_{2}=-\frac{9}{2},\qquad\ell_{3}=\frac{1159}{6}.

With these parameter values, we can solve the system necessary for similarity, i.e.

𝐐𝐂=𝐉𝐐,\displaystyle\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{C}=\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q},

to find that

𝐐=(19801011100),\displaystyle\mathbf{Q}=\begin{pmatrix}198&0&1\\ 0&1&1\\ 1&0&0\end{pmatrix},

which fulfills det⁡(𝐐)=−1≠0\det(\m{Q})=-1\neq 0.

Note that the matrix 𝐂\mathbf{C} has a principal submatrix 𝐒𝟏,𝟑\mathbf{S_{1,3}} with eigenvalues 124​(11±255383​i)\frac{1}{24}\left(11\pm\sqrt{255383}i\right), which are complex values with a positive real part, and hence our candidate submatrix to induce a wave instability.

Now we pick the diagonal matrix

𝔻=(δ0001000δ),\displaystyle\mathbb{D}=\begin{pmatrix}\delta&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&\delta\end{pmatrix},

to select the unstable principal submatrix of 𝐂\mathbf{C} we have designed via the parameter δ\delta, arriving at the diffusion matrix

𝐃^=𝐐​𝔻​𝐐−1=(δ00δ−11198​(1−δ)00δ).\displaystyle\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbb{D}\mathbf{Q}^{-1}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\delta&0&0\\ \delta-1&1&198(1-\delta)\\ 0&0&\delta\end{array}\right).

With this, we will be able to exhibit a wave instability, provided that δ\delta is small enough. In particular, if we let δ\delta range from 0 to 1 in discrete steps, we obtain the dispersion relations shown in Fig. 2. Note that the value given by the green dashed line corresponds to the asymptotic value of Re(λ)\real(\lambda) as μ→∞\mu\to\infty for the degenerate system at δ=0\delta=0, which corresponds to the real part of the eigenvalues of the unstable submatrix we designed in 𝐂\mathbf{C}. We plot the corresponding dispersion curve for δ=0\delta=0 in orange, noting that it is not an admissible value of δ\delta, as the linear system is ill-posed if Re(λ)>0\real(\lambda)>0 for arbitrarily large μ\mu. While this particular value is inadmissible, what we construct in this way is a dispersion relation that has the correct properties for all δ>0\delta>0. Note, in particular, that one can look at the curves between the red and the orange one (that is, δ∈(0,0.842742)\delta\in(0,0.842742)), and see that any of these intermediate values of δ\delta lead to the right form of a dispersion relation for a diffusion-driven instability. This is the key insight of Lemma 1 on which the constructions are based.

Hence, for sufficiently small δ>0\delta>0, we anticipate that the full system exhibits a wave instability. To ensure that the pattern is visible, i.e., that there is a nearby stable patterned state, we compute the criticality of both bifurcations, the traveling wave and the standing wave, using the approach outlined in [44]. The bifurcation for both, travelling and standing waves turns out to be supercritical in the set of values (b,δ)∈[0,1]×[0,1](b,\delta)\in[0,1]\times[0,1] on an infinite domain, indicating that they should be feasible to obtain via simulations. However, only the traveling wave turns out to be a stable pattern with periodic boundary conditions (see [45]), whilst the standing wave turns out to be stable in the presence of homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions. In particular, for δ=0.8\delta=0.8 we set the length of the domain as L=2.38​πL=2.38\pi and integrated the system with periodic boundary conditions. The solution we obtained is shown in Fig. 3, where we see that a travelling wave emerges from a smaller amplitude standing wave transient. We also integrated the system with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions to observe the solution shown in Fig. 4.

4.2 Hyperbolic reaction-diffusion system

We next provide an example based on a hyperbolic system. In [31], the authors study a general class of second order in time cross-diffusion systems. Such systems have particular motivations coming from understanding the microscopic inertia responsible for preventing the infinite speed of propagation that occurs in usual diffusion equations. See [34] for an overview of hyperbolic and other formulations of reaction-transport processes aiming to overcome this difficulty, and some of their connections with thermodynamic principles. They also arise as truncations or linearizations of some nonlocal-in-time systems, e.g. those due to fixed or distributed time delays arising in gene expression [59]. As an example of applying our constructions to these systems, we consider the following system from [31]:

τ​∂2u∂t2+∂u∂t=d11​∂2u∂x2+d12​∂2v∂x2+f⁡(u,v),\displaystyle\tau\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial t^{2}}+\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=d_{11}\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}+d_{12}\frac{\partial^{2}v}{\partial x^{2}}+f(u,v),
τ​∂2v∂t2+∂v∂t=d21​∂2u∂x2+d22​∂2v∂x2+g⁡(u,v),\displaystyle\tau\frac{\partial^{2}v}{\partial t^{2}}+\frac{\partial v}{\partial t}=d_{21}\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}+d_{22}\frac{\partial^{2}v}{\partial x^{2}}+g(u,v), (15)

with a particular choice of kinetics of FitzHugh-Nagumo type

f⁡(u,v)\displaystyle f(u,v) =u−a​u3+v−b,\displaystyle=u-au^{3}+v-b,
g⁡(u,v)\displaystyle g(u,v) =b−u−3​a​v.\displaystyle=b-u-3av.

This system turns out to be equivalent to a degenerate reaction-diffusion system given by

∂u∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} =w,\displaystyle=w,
∂v∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} =z,\displaystyle=z,
∂w∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial w}{\partial t} =1τ​(u−a​u3+v−b−w+d11​∂2u∂x2+d12​∂2v∂x2),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\tau}\left(u-au^{3}+v-b-w+d_{11}\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}+d_{12}\frac{\partial^{2}v}{\partial x^{2}}\right),
∂z∂t\displaystyle\frac{\partial z}{\partial t} =1τ​(b−u−3​a​v−z+d21​∂2u∂x2+d22​∂2v∂x2).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\tau}\left(b-u-3av-z+d_{21}\frac{\partial^{2}u}{\partial x^{2}}+d_{22}\frac{\partial^{2}v}{\partial x^{2}}\right).

While the analysis in [31] can be used to determine if a given set of parameters admits Turing or wave instabilities, the approach we use below allows us to constructively build a particular set of diffusion parameters (for a slightly modified system). Importantly, the method here generalizes to systems of n>2n>2 hyperbolic equations, though it is easier to see in this simplified setting.

The diffusion matrix is given by

𝐃^=(00000000d11τd12τ00d21τd22τ00).\displaystyle\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\ 0&0&0&0\\ \frac{d_{11}}{\tau}&\frac{d_{12}}{\tau}&0&0\\ \frac{d_{21}}{\tau}&\frac{d_{22}}{\tau}&0&0\end{pmatrix}.

As this system involves non-diffusible elements (see e.g. [60]), we cannot immediately apply the constructions developed throughout this article, as all the eigenvalues of D^\hat{D} are equal to zero for any diffusion rates. However, if we introduce a small change to this matrix, corresponding to a kind of parabolic perturbation, then we will be able to analyze it as a reaction-cross-diffusion system to produce Turing or wave instabilities using the theory we have developed. In particular, if we consider

𝐃^=(σ10000σ100d11τd12τσ20d21τd22τ0σ2),\displaystyle\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\begin{pmatrix}\sigma_{1}&0&0&0\\ 0&\sigma_{1}&0&0\\ \frac{d_{11}}{\tau}&\frac{d_{12}}{\tau}&\sigma_{2}&0\\ \frac{d_{21}}{\tau}&\frac{d_{22}}{\tau}&0&\sigma_{2}\end{pmatrix}, (16)

then

𝐃^=𝐐​𝔻​𝐐−1,\displaystyle\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbb{D}\mathbf{Q}^{-1},

If we make 𝜶𝟏,𝟐\boldsymbol{\alpha_{1,2}} unstable, we can take σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0 to generate a system with an instability and then increase that parameter a small amount (see Lemma 1). When setting σ1=0\sigma_{1}=0, we get

𝜶𝟏,𝟐=(−d22τ​σ2−d21τ​σ2−d12τ​σ2−d11τ​σ2).\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\alpha_{1,2}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-\frac{d_{22}}{\tau\sigma_{2}}&-\frac{d_{21}}{\tau\sigma_{2}}\\[4.30554pt] -\frac{d_{12}}{\tau\sigma_{2}}&-\frac{d_{11}}{\tau\sigma_{2}}\end{array}\right).

The only thing we need to do is to find parameters so that 𝜶𝟏,𝟐\boldsymbol{\alpha_{1,2}} is unstable. In particular, if we set

(d11,d12,d21,d22)=(−1,−1,0,−2),\displaystyle\left(d_{11},d_{12},d_{21},d_{22}\right)=\left(-1,-1,0,-2\right), (17)

then 𝜶𝟏,𝟐\boldsymbol{\alpha_{1,2}} becomes

(2001010),\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}20&0\\ 10&10\end{pmatrix},

which has positive real eigenvalues. We then take σ1=δ\sigma_{1}=\delta and vary this parameter to generate the dispersion relation shown in Fig. 5, where δ\delta goes from 0 to 2 in uniform steps of size 0.4. This graph is particularly interesting as it lets us see that, depending on the value of δ\delta, we find an interaction between Turing and wave instabilities (the eigenvalue with the largest real part is complex with a non-zero imaginary part for low values of kk but it becomes real for larger wavenumbers). Note that, for each δ\delta and kk, we are plotting the two eigenvalues with the largest real parts, which each coincide with the complex-conjugate pairs for small kk but bifurcate for larger kk into two strictly real branches. As before, the orange curves correspond to the inadmissible value of δ=0\delta=0, at which each curve tends to a different asymptotic eigenvalue shown in green lines. Again, we obtain the correct instability for those curves between the orange and red curves.

In particular, if we set homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, take δ=1.3\delta=1.3 with a domain length L=6L=6, and integrate the system, we obtain the pattern shown in Fig. 6. On the other hand, if we set periodic boundary conditions, with the same value of δ\delta, but a domain length L=30L=30 and integrate the system, we obtain the pattern shown in Fig. 7.

The solution uu in Fig. 6 takes negative values. This is not necessarily unphysical due to the nonlinearities being chosen to match a version of the FitzHugh-Nagumo model, where uu represents a membrane voltage, and hence its sign is not constrained. In other cases, however, one has to be careful using both hyperbolic terms or linear cross-diffusion to maintain positive solutions [34], as we will see in the next example.

In this example, we used Lemmas 1 and 2 to generate diffusion-driven instabilities in a reaction-diffusion system arising from a hyperbolic equation. This example is full of interesting features as some interactions between Turing and wave instabilities can be found. Some of these interactions can be explained by the use of (5, Theorem 4) for the matrix 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} instead of simply 𝐉\mathbf{J}.

4.3 3-component malaria model

In [5], the authors provided an example of a 3-component malaria model that was shown to be unable to exhibit Turing or wave instabilities for any diagonal diffusion matrix. We now show that we can generate diffusion-driven instabilities in this model if we consider chemotactic fluxes among the populations. In particular, we consider said system as

∂t𝐮=𝐟⁡(𝐮)+∂x(𝐃⁡(𝐮)​∂x𝐮),\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})+\partial_{x}\left(\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{u})\partial_{x}\mathbf{u}\right), (18)

where

𝐮=(H,I,P)⊺,𝐟⁡(𝐮)=((bH−dH)​H−c​P​H+r​I−dH​I+c​P​H−r​I−dM​P+b⁡(Q−P)​I),\displaystyle\mathbf{u}=(H,I,P)^{\intercal},\quad\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})=\begin{pmatrix}(b_{H}-d_{H})H-cPH+rI\\ -d_{H}I+cPH-rI\\ -d_{M}P+b(Q-P)I\end{pmatrix}, (19)

and the nonlinear diffusion tensor is given by

𝐃⁡(𝐮)=(D1,1χ⁡(HH∗)​D1,2χ⁡(HH∗)​D1,3χ⁡(II∗)​D2,1D2,2000D3,3),χ⁡(V)=2​V1+V2,\displaystyle\mathbf{D}(\mathbf{u})=\begin{pmatrix}D_{1,1}&\chi\left(\frac{H}{H^{*}}\right)D_{1,2}&\chi\left(\frac{H}{H^{*}}\right)D_{1,3}\\ \chi\left(\frac{I}{I^{*}}\right)D_{2,1}&D_{2,2}&0\\ 0&0&D_{3,3}\end{pmatrix},\quad\chi(V)=\frac{2V}{1+V^{2}}, (20)

The variables HH and II represent the populations of healthy and infected humans, respectively, whilst PP is the population of infected mosquitoes. Moreover, bHb_{H} represents the birth rate of healthy humans, dHd_{H} the death rate of humans, cc the infection rate between humans, rr the human recovery rate, dMd_{M} the death rate of infected mosquitoes, and bb is the infection rate between mosquitoes (see [61] for discussion of substantially more complicated compartment-based models of malaria transmission dynamics, from which the present model is a simplified albeit spatially-extended variant). Note that healthy mosquitoes do not appear explicitly in this model, as QQ represents the total (fixed) mosquito population, so Q−PQ-P is the population of healthy mosquitoes.

We interpret the cross-diffusion terms as chemotactic fluxes [62] with saturating sensitivities corresponding to volume-filling effects [63]. This represents populations moving along signalling gradients of the other populations. We have assumed several zeros in the diffusion matrix as we do not expect mosquitoes’ spatial movements to be largely influenced directly by human populations. To fix ideas, we will focus on generating Turing instabilities by varying the diffusion matrix, with a constrained diffusion tensor having the form given by Eq. 21. The variables H∗H^{*} and I∗I^{*} represent homogeneous steady-state values of these parameters. Due to the choice of the sensitivity function χ\chi, we have that χ⁡(1)=1\chi(1)=1. Hence, after linearizing around such a homogeneous steady state, we have the linear diffusion tensor:

This system has only two equilibria, 𝟎=(0,0,0)\mathbf{0}=(0,0,0) and 𝐏=(H∗,I∗,P∗)\mathbf{P}=\left(H^{*},I^{*},P^{*}\right), where

We show examples of two-dimensional plots obtained in Fig. 9, where the small perturbation of the homogeneous equilibrium relaxes to a stationary pattern over time. We remark that the choice of nonlinear diffusion here was motivated in part because linear cross-diffusion terms will not ensure that the variables remain positive, breaking both the boundedness of the solutions due to the quadratic nonlinearities and the physical interpretations of the state variables as populations. Nevertheless, the theory developed here is immediately applicable to suitable parameterized forms of nonlinear diffusion as shown in this example.

4.4 Keller-Segel model

One major motivation for cross-diffusion systems is the well-known Keller-Segel model for chemotaxis (see [64, 24], and references therein). Here, we provide an example showing how we can use Theorem 2 to generate diffusion-driven instabilities. We consider a three-species formulation (again to allow for wave instabilities) given by

∂t𝐮=𝐟(𝐮)+∇⋅(𝐃∇𝐮),\displaystyle\partial_{t}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf{D}\nabla\mathbf{u}), (24)

where

𝐟⁡(𝐮)=(b​u​(1−u)c​u+e​v+f​w−ε​v3g​u+h​v+j​w−ε​w3),and𝐃=(d−2​a​u1+u20010001),\displaystyle\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})=\begin{pmatrix}bu(1-u)\\ cu+ev+fw-\varepsilon v^{3}\\ gu+hv+jw-\varepsilon w^{3}\end{pmatrix},\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbf{D}=\begin{pmatrix}d&-\frac{2au}{1+u^{2}}&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}, (25)

with b,c,e,f,g,h,j∈ℝb,c,e,f,g,h,j\in\mathbb{R} being parameters of the reaction of the system, a,d>0a,d>0 being associated with the diffusion of the species in the system, and 0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1. In this example, we will assume that dd is fixed and we need to construct 𝐉\mathbf{J} to obtain Turing and wave instabilities with a constrained Jacobian matrix having the form given by Eq. 26. We remark that the cubic nonlinearities in the equations for vv and ww are used solely to bound solutions, with linear interactions chosen for simplicity, but one can view the forthcoming linear analysis as applicable to other 3-species variations of these reaction kinetics.

If we focus on the homogeneous steady state given by 𝐏=(1,0,0)⊺\mathbf{P}=(1,0,0)^{\intercal}, then

𝐉=(−b00cefghj),and𝐃^=(d−a0010001).\displaystyle\mathbf{J}=\begin{pmatrix}-b&0&0\\ c&e&f\\ g&h&j\end{pmatrix},\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\begin{pmatrix}d&-a&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&1\end{pmatrix}. (26)

Here, we consider d≠1d\neq 1 to ensure that 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} is diagonalizable. With this, we have

𝐃^=𝐐​𝔻​𝐐−1,\displaystyle\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbb{D}\mathbf{Q}^{-1},

where

𝐐=(0ad−11010100),𝔻=diag⁡{1,1,d}.\displaystyle\mathbf{Q}=\begin{pmatrix}0&&\frac{a}{d-1}&&1\\[8.61108pt] 0&&1&&0\\ 1&&0&&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad\mathbb{D}=\diag\left\{1,1,d\right\}.

Therefore, we have that

𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐=(ja​gd−1+hgfa​cd−1+ec−a​fd−1−a⁡(a​c+b​d−b+(d−1)​e)(d−1)2−b−a​cd−1),\displaystyle\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q}=\begin{pmatrix}j&&\frac{ag}{d-1}+h&&g\\[8.61108pt] f&&\frac{ac}{d-1}+e&&c\\[8.61108pt] -\frac{af}{d-1}&&-\frac{a(ac+bd-b+(d-1)e)}{(d-1)^{2}}&&-b-\dfrac{ac}{d-1}\end{pmatrix},

which has the following eigenvalues:

λ1\displaystyle\lambda_{1} =−b,\displaystyle=-b,
λ±\displaystyle\lambda_{\pm} =e+j±(e+i)2−4​(e​i−f​h)2.\displaystyle=\frac{e+j\pm\sqrt{(e+i)^{2}-4(ei-fh)}}{2}.

This entails that, to make this matrix stable, we need to have b>0b>0, e+j<0e+j<0, and e​j−f​h>0ej-fh>0. Now, we fix a=3a=3. With this, we have two cases:

The case d<1d<1:

In this case, following Lemma 9, as there is only one entry in 𝔻\mathbb{D} with the lowest value located in the lower right corner, we have that the eigenvalues of 𝐉−μ​𝐃^\mathbf{J}-\mu\mathbf{\hat{D}} will be led by the bottom right entry of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} when said entry is large. For example, if we consider d=0.9d=0.9, and consider the parameters

(b,c,e,f,g,h,j)=(1,36.7,−32,−1,−1.5,−1618,−64),\displaystyle(b,c,e,f,g,h,j)=(1,36.7,-32,-1,-1.5,-1618,-64), (27)

we have that the bottom right element of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} equals 1100>01100>0. This gives rise to the dispersion relation shown in Fig. 10. This shows that we have generated a diffusion-driven instability for the parameter values chosen. Furthermore, when k=5k=5, we have that λmax=20.4439∈ℝ\lambda_{\max}=20.4439\in\mathbb{R}, which implies that we are seeing a Turing instability.

Furthermore, to check our prediction, we integrated the system numerically and obtained the solution shown in Fig. 11. The solution initially forms a series of spikes that merge, eventually tending towards peaks commonly seen in Keller-Segel type models more generally [64, 65].

The case d>1d>1:

In this case, once again following Lemma 9, as there are two entries in 𝔻\mathbb{D} with the lowest value, we can make the 1, 2-submatrix of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} unstable on a large scale to produce wave instabilities. In particular, if we consider d=1.1d=1.1 and

(b,c,e,f,g,h,j)=(8,33.75,−512.5,−500,−0.41922,512.577,500),\displaystyle(b,c,e,f,g,h,j)=(8,33.75,-512.5,-500,-0.41922,512.577,500), (28)

we get that this principal submatrix will be given by

(500500−500500),\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}500&500\\ -500&500\end{pmatrix},

which is unstable with two complex conjugate eigenvalues. This gives rise to the dispersion relation shown in Fig. 12, which shows that we have generated a diffusion-driven instability for the parameter values chosen. Furthermore, when k=4k=4, we have that λmax=26.1765±75.7567​i∈ℂ\lambda_{\max}=26.1765\pm 75.7567i\in\mathbb{C}, which implies that we are seeing a wave instability.

Once again, to check the outcome of the design process we have carried out, we integrated the system with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions for these parameter values. In Fig. 13, we show a solution leading to spatiotemporal oscillations, which is an outcome one expects from a wave instability [44].

In many instances of Keller-Segel-type models, the value of dd is equal to 1. That case is degenerate because the leading submatrix becomes non-diagonalizable for that value of dd. In any case, just by continuity, one can continue the bifurcation using numerical continuation software and still get diffusion-driven instabilities when d=1d=1.

5 Discussion

We have developed an approach to designing reaction-cross-diffusion systems exhibiting Turing or wave instabilities for systems involving several components. We showed how to constructively build unstable principal submatrices which essentially encode these instabilities, and place these within the design constraints of a given system. The assumptions in Theorems 1 and 2 are rather mild, suggesting that this process can be employed for large classes of systems, leaving flexibility in the constructions to allow for additional design constraints if they arise. This demonstrates some of the freedom gained in allowing non-diagonal diffusion tensors, or in having complete control over linearized kinetics. Finally, we showed these ideas in four distinct models with a range of linear and nonlinear transport, highlighting further issues of model construction that may arise, such as in preventing blowups or ensuring the positivity of solutions when this is required. We remark that all but the first example demonstrated employing these ideas in cases where we did not allow complete freedom over either matrix in the linearization, but instead had to work in a more constrained setting. An important thermodynamic consideration is to restrict to diffusion matrices 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} that are symmetric, as these can more easily be justified from the thermodynamic perspective [66]. In such cases, Theorem 2 can be applied directly, although the constructions used in proving Theorem 1 would require significant changes that we leave for future work.

There are numerous future directions from the work carried out here. One could try to generalize Theorem 2 by assuming that the diffusion matrix 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} admits complex eigenvalues. While such matrices are easier to work with in some sense (the set of diagonalizable matrices is dense in the set of invertible matrices), complex eigenvalues would require more care in carrying out the procedure given in Lemma 1, and hence may require entirely different constructions to arrive at something like Theorem 2. In a different direction, one could consider evolution equations with nonlocal spatial operators. Such integro-differential equations show stark differences with their classical local counterparts, allowing for spatiotemporal pattern formation in scalar models [67], and showing dependence on the geometry not exhibited by local models even in the linear stability theory [68]. Such cases are more intricate as the symbol of the operator (i.e. the function of the wavenumber one obtains from the linearization in spectral space) is no longer a polynomial in general. Thus, developing an analogue of the procedure presented here would be substantially more involved. In contrast, the results we have presented essentially apply even to reaction-cross-diffusion systems posed on general Riemannian manifolds or even networks, modulo finite-size effects (8, Section 3).

Although the linear theory developed is useful, Turing and wave instabilities do not ensure on their own that one will always be able to find specific kinds of solutions emerging from the instability of a spatially homogeneous equilibrium. We focused on the instability of a single homogeneous steady state, but realistic systems may admit more than one such state, leading to cases where the linear theory fails to capture the emergence of patterning due to other attracting states [69]. As we showed in the first example, calculations of the criticality of the bifurcations can be invaluable to ensure that a nearby stable pattern exists in the case of a supercritical bifurcation. In contrast, a subcritical bifurcation is a situation where the linear theory is not always a good indicator of subsequent emergent behaviour [4, 57, 70, 44]. We note, in particular, that the two-species Keller-Segel model with logistic growth can exhibit spatiotemporal chaos after a subcritical Turing instability, despite such two-species systems not exhibiting wave instabilities or even Hopf bifurcations of homogeneous states [65] (though see [71, 72] for cases where patterned states undergo Hopf bifurcations leading to these spatiotemporal behaviours). Hence, there is substantial work to be done in building design principles that extend to the weakly nonlinear setting, and even developing a language of constraints for nonlinearities. Related to this limitation, the assumption of homogeneous Neumann or periodic conditions precludes the interplay of more complex boundary conditions which can modify patterns and even initiate patterning outside of the Turing space determined here via linear theory [46, 47].

In a different direction, we note that, depending on the purpose of the mathematical model, having too much freedom in the design can lead to unsatisfying theories. Given full control over the nonlinearities, one can design even two-component reaction-diffusion systems that exhibit a wide variety of pre-defined behaviours [42, 73], with essentially the freedom to match any kind of patterned state. Given such freedom, one must impose constraints that involve both linear and nonlinear aspects of the system under study to ensure that the choices made make sense in the modelling context. Similarly, while the results we have presented are general and powerful, one can argue that they provide too much freedom. In particular, there are few systems where one has complete control over either transport or reactions. Nevertheless, experimental protocols are increasingly providing more ways to create and tune a number of systems to exhibit patterning [74, 37, 75], and the fundamental routes to instabilities provided here can provide some guidance on pursuing these in increasingly sophisticated systems even under constraints. Importantly, we note that the ideas used apply even with more constraints in the given system, as shown in the examples.

Appendix A Useful results for designing unstable systems

Here, we collect a few additional lemmas that provide alternative ways of viewing the constructions illustrated above. In practice, particularly given additional constraints (i.e. when one does not have complete freedom over 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} or 𝐉\mathbf{J}), these results can help one find parameters to exhibit Turing or wave instabilities. We begin by showing that Lemma 1 has a converse, implying that, for a diagonalizable diffusion tensor, the existence of a principle unstable submatrix of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} is both necessary and sufficient for diffusion-driven instability.

The authors in (21, Theorem 1) state that, when the diffusion matrix of a reaction-diffusion system is diagonal and the Jacobian matrix of the system in the absence of diffusion is S-stable, then the system does not admit Turing instabilities. In the proof of (5, Theorem 2), the authors noted that the original proof also applies to wave instabilities. We can directly use this result to obtain an equivalent statement in the case of reaction-cross-diffusion systems, as in the case of a non-diagonal 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}}.

The growth rates (eigenvalues) of the original system given in Eq. 2 are equivalent to those of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q}. Hence by directly applying (5, Theorem 2) to this system, we have the following Lemma:

Lemma 6.

Assuming that 𝐃^=𝐐​𝔻​𝐐−1\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbb{D}\mathbf{Q}^{-1} is diagonalizable with non-negative real eigenvalues, and 𝐉\mathbf{J} is a stable matrix, then if 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} is an S-stable matrix, the system Eq. 2 does not admit Turing or wave instabilities.

The proofs of Section 2.1 and Section 2.2 both relied on the use of Lemma 1, where some diffusion coefficients were taken to be zero in an asymptotic limit. We can instead use an alternative approach where some diffusion coefficients tend to infinity instead. We can obtain this as a corollary of (5, Lemma 6) applied to the diagonalized system 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q}.

Lemma 7.

Let 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} be a diagonalizable matrix with non-negative real eigenvalues. Assume that 𝐃^\mathbf{\hat{D}} has ℓ\ell eigenvalues σi1,…,σiℓ\sigma_{i_{1}},\ldots,\sigma_{i_{\ell}} that tend to ∞\infty, while all the others remain positive but finite. Then, there exist ℓ\ell eigenvalues of 𝐉−μ​𝐃^\mathbf{J}-\mu\mathbf{\hat{D}} having real parts that tend to −∞-\infty for every μ>0\mu>0, while n−ℓn-\ell eigenvalues of said matrix tend to the eigenvalues of the principal submatrix of 𝐐−1​𝐉𝐐\mathbf{Q}^{-1}\mathbf{J}\mathbf{Q} formed out of the rows and columns that are complementary to i1,…,iℓi_{1},\ldots,i_{\ell}, as μ→0+\mu\to 0^{+}.

Next, we develop two lemmas useful in dealing with systems that have constraints (i.e. ones where we cannot control every element of 𝐃\mathbf{D} or 𝐉\mathbf{J}). By an elementary formula (see, e.g. (76, Equation (1))), we have the following result.

Lemma 8.

Let λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}. Then

det⁡(𝐉−λ​𝐈n)\displaystyle\det\left(\mathbf{J}-\lambda\mathbf{I}_{n}\right) =bn​λn+bn−1​λn−1+bn−2​λn−2+…​b1​λ+b0,\displaystyle=b_{n}\lambda^{n}+b_{n-1}\lambda^{n-1}+b_{n-2}\lambda^{n-2}+\ldots b_{1}\lambda+b_{0}, (29)

where

Lemma 8 enables us to prove a general result that can be used to generate Turing and wave instabilities in systems with more constraints. To motivate the coming result, we note that although Remark 1 helped us prove the general results stated in Theorem 1, we can provide a generalization of this idea that let us embed larger unstable principal submatrices within the Jacobian matrix of the system via similarity. Furthermore, as we have already seen, there are cases in which different interactions between Turing and wave instabilities can occur, and being able to directly design such instances can be done using this generalization. For example, consider the Jacobian matrix given by

𝐉=(−21.3−78.28747.4−11−35−3.13),\displaystyle\mathbf{J}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}-21.3&-78.2&87\\ 47.4&-1&1\\ -35&-3.1&3\end{array}\right),

which has eigenvalues −9.50278±81.3221​i,−0.29445-9.50278\pm 81.3221i,-0.29445, meaning it is stable. We note that it has a 2×22\times 2 unstable principal submatrix at the bottom-right corner with eigenvalues 0.05131670.0513167 and 1.948681.94868, with an element within this submatrix being 3. In particular, if we consider a diffusion matrix given by

𝐃^=(1000000.0001000δ),\displaystyle\mathbf{\hat{D}}=\begin{pmatrix}100&0&0\\ 0&0.0001&0\\ 0&0&\delta\end{pmatrix}, (33)

the dispersion relation of a potential system we can generate with these matrices for different values of δ\delta that range from 0 to 0.002 in uniform steps of size 0.0004 is shown in Fig. 14. Here, we note that there is a strong interaction between Turing and wave instabilities. In fact, when δ=0\delta=0, the largest eigenvalue converges to a real number as k→∞k\to\infty, as it is expected. However, for larger values of δ\delta, there is an interaction between real and complex-conjugate eigenvalues as there is a range of values of said parameter under which two complex conjugate eigenvalues split into two real eigenvalues for a range of values of kk. This implies that several different scenarios can be generated through different unstable submatrices in the Jacobian matrix of the system. The question is then how can we generate a stable matrix from an unstable one? Part of the answer is provided in the following lemma, which once again, allows for several degrees of freedom.

To introduce the following result, let 𝐊\mathbf{K} be a square matrix of size ℓ×ℓ\ell\times\ell. Furthermore, let 𝐒𝐢𝟏,…,𝐢𝐦\mathbf{S_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}}} be its principal submatrix comprising only its i1,…,imi_{1},\ldots,i_{m} rows and columns and Mi1,…,imM_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}} its determinant. Furthermore, for p,q∈{1,…,m}p,q\in\{1,\ldots,m\}, we denote by 𝐒𝐢𝟏,…,𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐩,𝐢𝐪\mathbf{S_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}}^{i_{p},i_{q}}} the submatrix of 𝐒𝐢𝟏,…,𝐢𝐦\mathbf{S_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}}} after extracting its ipi_{p}-th row and iqi_{q}-th column, and Mi1,…,imip,iqM_{i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}}^{i_{p},i_{q}} again denotes the corresponding determinant. We then have the following result.

Let ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1 be an integer and let 𝐀\mathbf{A} be a matrix of size (ℓ+1)×(ℓ+1)(\ell+1)\times(\ell+1) with ℓ+1\ell+1 different eigenvalues. Proof.

As the eigenvalues of 𝐀\mathbf{A} are all different, then a matrix is similar to 𝐀\mathbf{A} if and only if it has the same characteristic polynomial as 𝐀\mathbf{A}. By Lemma 8, the characteristic polynomial of BB is given by

On the other hand, the characteristic polynomial of 𝐀\mathbf{A} has the same form with different coefficients:

While the precise forms of these similarity matrices arise in applying the result given in Theorem 1, their constructions are a bit tedious and substantially easier to obtain using a computer algebra system. Importantly, we only need such constructions to arrive at the result given in Lemma 3, and note that this can be satisfied using other constructions as well.
